questions.questionText: The SI unit of electric charge is:
questions.explanation: Electric charge is measured in coulomb (C), which is the SI unit of charge.

questions.questionText: According to Coulomb's law, the electrostatic force between two point charges is directly proportional to:
questions.explanation: Coulomb's law states that F ∝ q₁q₂/r².

questions.questionText: The value of Coulomb's constant (k = 1/4πε₀) in vacuum is approximately:
questions.explanation: The electrostatic constant k in vacuum is approximately 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².

questions.questionText: Like charges always:
questions.explanation: Charges of the same sign repel each other, while unlike charges attract.

questions.questionText: Electric field at a point is defined as:

options.text: Force experienced by a unit positive test charge

questions.explanation: Electric field strength is the force acting on a unit positive test charge placed at that point.

questions.questionText: The SI unit of electric field is:
questions.explanation: Electric field is force per unit charge, so its SI unit is N/C.

questions.questionText: Electric field lines originate from:
questions.explanation: Electric field lines start from positive charges and terminate on negative charges.

questions.questionText: The electric field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is:
questions.explanation: Free charges redistribute themselves until the electric field inside the conductor becomes zero.

questions.questionText: Two point charges +2 μC and +3 μC are separated by 2 m in vacuum. The electrostatic force between them is:
If the distance between two point charges is doubled while keeping the charges unchanged, the electrostatic force becomes:
questions.explanation: Since F ∝ 1/r², doubling the distance reduces the force to one-fourth.

questions.questionText: A point charge of +5 μC produces an electric field at a point 3 m away. The magnitude of the electric field is:
The electric field due to a negative point charge is directed:
questions.explanation: Electric field lines terminate on negative charges, so the field points towards the charge.

questions.questionText: According to the principle of superposition, the resultant electric force on a charge is:

options.text: The product of all individual forces
The scalar sum of magnitudes only
The vector sum of individual forces

questions.explanation: Electric forces obey the principle of superposition, so they add vectorially.

questions.questionText: The electric flux through a closed surface depends on:

options.text: The total charge enclosed by the surface
The shape of the surface only
The area of the surface only
The electric field outside the surface only

questions.explanation: Gauss's law states that net electric flux through a closed surface depends only on the enclosed charge.

questions.questionText: The SI unit of electric flux is:
questions.explanation: Electric flux = Electric field × Area, so its SI unit is N·m²/C.

questions.questionText: A charge of +8 μC is enclosed inside a closed surface. The net electric flux through the surface is closest to:
A Gaussian surface encloses equal positive and negative charges. The net electric flux through the surface is:
questions.explanation: Equal positive and negative enclosed charges give zero net enclosed charge, so the net flux is zero.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements about electric field lines is incorrect?
questions.explanation: Electrostatic field lines begin on positive charges and end on negative charges; they do not form closed loops.

questions.questionText: If the magnitude of one point charge is doubled and the distance between two charges is also doubled, the electrostatic force between them becomes:
questions.explanation: Since F ∝ q/r², the new force is (2)/(2²) = 1/2 of the original force.

questions.questionText: An electric dipole is placed in a uniform electric field. If the dipole axis is perpendicular to the field, the torque on the dipole is:
questions.explanation: Torque on a dipole is τ = pE sinθ. It is maximum when θ = 90°.
